title: India, Japan Air Chiefs Fly Tejas Formation Sortie in Veer Guardian 2026
excerpt: Air Chief Marshal AP Singh led the formation while JASDF chief General Takehiro Morita flew in a Tejas trainer at Jodhpur, capping the first-ever deployment of Japanese fighters to India.
body:
• Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh and Japan Air Self-Defense Force Chief of Staff General Takehiro Morita flew a Tejas formation sortie at Air Force Station Jodhpur on Sunday during Exercise Veer Guardian-2026.
  • Singh led the formation in a Tejas fighter; Morita flew in a trainer aircraft captained by Group Captain I Samrat, commanding officer of the Tejas squadron.
  • The exercise, running September 9–22, 2026, is the second India-Japan air drill — and the first to see Japanese F-2A fighters deployed to Indian soil.
  • Defence Minister Rajnath Singh earlier called Japan's deployment of fighters to India a "significant milestone" for the bilateral defence partnership.

Two Chiefs, One Formation

The chiefs of the Indian Air Force and the Japan Air Self-Defense Force took to the skies together on Sunday, flying a formation sortie in India's indigenous Light Combat Aircraft Tejas at Air Force Station Jodhpur. Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh, the IAF's Chief of the Air Staff, flew a Tejas fighter and led the formation; General Takehiro Morita, Chief of Staff of the JASDF, flew in a trainer aircraft captained by Group Captain I Samrat, the commanding officer of the Tejas squadron.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HTq12lTUYYQ

The formation flew over the airfield before executing a peel-off manoeuvre for landing, according to the IAF. The sortie was staged during the ongoing bilateral air exercise Veer Guardian-2026, and the IAF said it gave Morita a first-hand experience of the Tejas and its systems while giving the two chiefs a rare opportunity for professional interaction in the cockpit rather than the conference room.

Context & Background

Veer Guardian-2026 is the second edition of the India-Japan bilateral air exercise — the first was held in Japan in 2023 — and it is being conducted at Jodhpur from September 9 to 22, 2026. The IAF is participating with a mix of frontline combat aircraft: the indigenous LCA Tejas, the Su-30MKI and the Rafale. Japan has deployed its F-2A fighters, ferried from Tsuiki Air Base along with the Japanese contingent and support equipment.

The headline significance of this edition is where it is being held. It is the first time Japanese fighter aircraft have deployed to India for a bilateral exercise — a step Defence Minister Rajnath Singh described on September 10 as a "significant milestone" for the India-Japan defence partnership. In a post on X, Singh said the maiden visit of JASDF fighters to India reflected growing trust and a shared commitment to peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific, recalling his "highly productive discussions" with his Japanese counterpart in New Delhi the previous month.

The exercise, now in its final phase, involves operational flying, advanced mission planning, air-strike missions, simulated combat scenarios, and professional exchanges covering engineering and aerospace safety — aimed at tactical proficiency and operational synergy between forces that fly different platforms under different doctrines.

"I will remember it not only as a truly valuable experience, but also as a powerful symbol of trust, confidence and friendship."

— General Takehiro Morita, Chief of Staff, JASDF

Impact & Analysis

A joint flight by two service chiefs is theatre with a purpose. Fighter diplomacy of this kind — the same playbook India has used with French and American counterparts — signals political trust at the operational level, and putting Morita in the back seat of a Tejas is as much a product demonstration as a courtesy. The Tejas, built by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, is the centrepiece of India's pitch as an indigenous aerospace power, and every foreign officer who flies it becomes a data point in that campaign.

Morita's remarks at the joint press interaction pointed to where the partnership is heading. He said cooperation had moved beyond holding exercises together to refining tactical capabilities at a practical level, with exchanges running from senior officers down to subject-matter experts — and floated possible cooperation in space. Singh, for his part, described the relationship as "a partnership built on mutual respect, professional trust, and shared commitment to peace and stability," invoking Kizuna — the Japanese concept of enduring bonds built on mutual trust and support — and reiterating the shared vision of a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific.

The timing is not incidental. With the exercise concluding on September 22, the chiefs' sortie caps a fortnight designed to prove that Indian and Japanese air power can plan, fly and fight together — a message aimed as much at the region as at each other.

Diaspora Angle

The Indian diaspora in Japan — a community of over 40,000, concentrated in Tokyo, Yokohama and Kobe — watches the defence relationship as a proxy for how seriously Tokyo takes New Delhi. Each visible milestone, from the first Veer Guardian in Japan to Japanese fighters landing at Jodhpur, reinforces the community's standing in a country where Indians remain a small but fast-growing minority. Beyond that, diaspora defence-watchers track the Tejas with proprietary pride: an indigenous fighter carrying a foreign air chief is exactly the image of "Make in India" they share back home.

What's Next

Veer Guardian-2026 wraps up on September 22, after which both air forces will debrief the fortnight's missions and feed the lessons into the next edition. The trajectory is clear: from a first exercise on Japanese soil in 2023, to Japanese fighters on Indian soil in 2026, to — if Morita's space-cooperation hint is any indication — domains beyond the atmosphere. The chiefs' Tejas flight was the symbol; the substance will be in whatever the two staffs schedule next.
